items.q: No sooner (A) the whistle had blown than the two captains (B) shook hands and (C) took up their positions on (D) the muddy pitch.
items.explanation: After a negative adverbial such as No sooner the auxiliary must be inverted with the subject: No sooner had the whistle blown than.

items.q: The examiners (A) demanded that every candidate (B) submits a handwritten essay, (C) whereas the deputy head (D) favoured typed work.
items.explanation: Verbs of demand and suggestion (demand, insist, suggest, recommend) are followed by the bare subjunctive: demanded that every candidate submit.

items.q: (A) Having missed the last ferry, (B) the travellers had no choice but (C) spending the night in (D) a draughty harbour café.
options: the travellers had no choice but
items.explanation: The fixed expression is have no choice but to do something; the participle spending cannot follow but here.

items.q: If the engineers (A) had checked the dam's foundations (B) more thoroughly last spring, the valley (C) below it (D) would not have been flooding now.
options: would not have been flooding now
items.explanation: A mixed conditional pairs a past condition (had checked) with a present result marked by now, so the main clause takes would + be + -ing, not the past-perfect form.

items.q: I wish I (A) have paid more attention (B) when my grandfather (C) tried to teach me (D) how to graft apple trees.
items.explanation: A regret about the past after wish takes the past perfect: I wish I had paid, never the present perfect.

items.q: It was (A) not until the final chapter (B) when the detective revealed (C) who had been sending (D) the anonymous letters.
items.explanation: A cleft sentence beginning It was not until… is completed by that, not by when: It was not until the final chapter that the detective revealed…

items.q: The museum (A) received so much praise for its new exhibition that (B) extra staff and (C) a large number of equipment (D) had to be hired to control the crowds.
items.explanation: Equipment is uncountable, so it takes a large amount of / a great deal of; a large number of is reserved for plural countable nouns.

items.q: The lecture on volcanic activity (A) proved so absorbing that (B) hardly anyone noticed (C) the time, and the audience stayed for (D) so a long discussion afterwards.
items.explanation: Before a/an + adjective + noun the intensifier is such (such a long discussion); so goes directly before an adjective or adverb alone.

items.q: (A) Scarcely the plane had left the runway when (B) a flock of geese (C) forced the pilot (D) to turn back to the terminal.
options: Scarcely the plane had left the runway
to turn back to the terminal
items.correction: Scarcely had the plane left the runway
items.explanation: When Scarcely opens the sentence, subject and auxiliary invert: Scarcely had the plane left… when….

items.q: My sister (A) prefers to sketch in charcoal, (B) despite I find watercolours (C) far more forgiving (D) of a beginner's mistakes.
items.explanation: The sentence contrasts two preferences, which needs the conjunction whereas/while; despite is a preposition and cannot introduce a clause.

items.q: The marathon (A) went ahead as planned (B) on Sunday morning (C) despite the forecast had warned of (D) torrential rain along the coast.
options: despite the forecast had warned of
items.correction: although the forecast had warned of
items.explanation: Despite must be followed by a noun or -ing form; a full clause with subject and verb requires although/even though.

items.q: The new science syllabus (A) requires pupils (B) to design an experiment, (C) recording their observations, and (D) to present the results to the class.
options: to present the results to the class
items.explanation: Items in a list must be parallel: the other two are infinitives (to design… to present), so the middle item must be to record, not an -ing form.

items.q: (A) Not having eaten since dawn, (B) the smell of fresh bread (C) proved irresistible to (D) the exhausted hikers.
items.correction: As they had not eaten since dawn
items.explanation: A participle clause must share the subject of the main clause; here it wrongly attaches to the smell (a dangling modifier), so a full clause with its own subject is needed.

items.q: Although the twins (A) look identical, their teachers (B) can easily say them apart (C) by the way (D) each one holds a pen.
items.explanation: The phrasal verb meaning to distinguish two similar people is tell apart; say does not form this collocation.

items.q: Only when the last guest (A) had departed (B) Mrs Tran allowed herself (C) to sit down (D) with a cup of tea.
items.explanation: When Only when introduces the first clause, the main clause is inverted: Only when… did Mrs Tran allow herself….

items.q: The nutritionist (A) suggested that the canteen (B) replace fried snacks (C) with fruit, and that (D) sugary drinks were removed altogether.
items.explanation: Both clauses depend on suggested that, so both take the subjunctive: the canteen replace… and that sugary drinks be removed.

items.q: (A) Rarely has the townspeople witnessed (B) such a violent storm as (C) the one that (D) tore through the valley last August.
options: tore through the valley last August
items.explanation: Inversion does not change agreement: the plural subject the townspeople still needs the plural auxiliary have.

items.q: The scientist (A) who the committee believed (B) deserved the prize was passed over in favour of (C) a colleague (D) whom, it later emerged, had falsified his data.
options: whom, it later emerged, had falsified his data
items.correction: who, it later emerged, had falsified his data
items.explanation: The relative pronoun is the subject of had falsified (the comment it later emerged is parenthetical), so it must be who, not the object form whom.

items.q: Of all the cyclists (A) who entered the race, Linh was (B) by far the (C) more experienced, having (D) competed abroad on several occasions.
items.explanation: Comparing one person with all the others (of all the cyclists) needs the superlative the most experienced; the comparative is for two.

items.q: The guide (A) warned us that (B) the tide would come in quickly (C) and asked (D) had anyone swum in open water before.
options: the tide would come in quickly
had anyone swum in open water before
items.correction: whether anyone had swum in open water before
items.explanation: A reported yes/no question is introduced by whether/if and keeps statement word order: asked whether anyone had swum, with no inversion.

items.q: (A) The most people (B) who visit the night market (C) come for the grilled seafood (D) rather than the souvenirs.
items.explanation: Most meaning 'the majority of' takes no article: Most people; the most is only used for the superlative.

items.q: The committee (A) has finally agreed (B) in a date for the exhibition, (C) which will feature (D) works by local sculptors.
options: in a date for the exhibition
items.correction: on a date for the exhibition
items.explanation: You agree on (or agree upon) a decision such as a date; agree in is not the collocation.

items.q: By the time the rescue helicopter (A) reached the stranded climbers, they (B) had spent two nights on the ledge and (C) have run out of food (D) the previous evening.
options: had spent two nights on the ledge
items.explanation: Both events happened before the past moment by the time the helicopter reached, so both verbs take the past perfect: had spent… and had run out.

items.q: The village (A) where my grandparents grew up, (B) which lies beside a bend in the river, (C) is known for its pottery, (D) most of them is sold abroad.
options: which lies beside a bend in the river
most of them is sold abroad
items.correction: most of which is sold abroad
items.explanation: A clause added with a comma needs a relative pronoun to link it: most of which (referring to pottery); most of them would create a run-on sentence.

items.q: (A) The rapid expand of online tutoring (B) has left some parents wondering (C) whether traditional classrooms (D) will survive the decade.
options: The rapid expand of online tutoring
items.correction: The rapid expansion of online tutoring
items.explanation: After an article and adjective (the rapid …) a noun is required, so the verb expand must be nominalised as expansion.

items.q: (A) Had the goalkeeper (B) not been slipped on the wet turf, (C) the match would have ended (D) in a goalless draw.
options: not been slipped on the wet turf
items.correction: not slipped on the wet turf
items.explanation: The inverted third conditional is Had + subject + (not) + past participle; slip is intransitive, so there is no passive been slipped.

items.q: The storm (A) brought (B) such strong winds that (C) so many damage was done (D) to the orchard's oldest trees.
items.explanation: Damage is an uncountable noun, so it takes much: so much damage; many is only for plural countables.

items.q: (A) No matter how carefully (B) the recipe is followed, the soufflé (C) will collapse (D) unless the oven door is not kept shut.
options: unless the oven door is not kept shut
items.correction: unless the oven door is kept shut
items.explanation: Unless already means if… not, so the clause after it must be positive: unless the door is kept shut; a second not reverses the meaning.

items.q: (A) Hardly had the curtain risen than (B) a spotlight suddenly failed, (C) plunging the stage (D) into total darkness.
options: Hardly had the curtain risen than
items.correction: Hardly had the curtain risen when
items.explanation: Hardly/Scarcely pairs with when; it is No sooner that pairs with than.

items.q: The archivist (A) drew our attention to a letter (B) which sheds light in (C) the poet's final months (D) in exile.
options: drew our attention to a letter
items.explanation: The idiom meaning 'to help explain' is shed light on something; the preposition is fixed.

items.q: The council (A) has promised that (B) by next spring the new library (C) has been completed, (D) although few residents believe it.
options: by next spring the new library
items.explanation: The promise concerns the future (by next spring), so the present perfect has been completed is impossible; completion before a future point takes the future perfect passive will have been completed (or simply will be completed).

items.q: (A) Having been delayed by fog, the flight (B) finally landed at midnight, (C) leaving dozens of passengers (D) stranding without a connection.
items.explanation: The passengers do not do the stranding; they are left in that state, so the past participle stranded is needed after leaving dozens of passengers.

items.q: (A) Neither the coach nor the players was willing to (B) comment on the defeat, (C) though rumours of a rift (D) had been circulating for weeks.
options: Neither the coach nor the players was willing to
items.correction: Neither the coach nor the players were willing to
items.explanation: With neither… nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject; the players is plural, so the verb is were.

items.q: The two rival bakeries (A) on Le Loi Street (B) have been competing with themselves for decades, (C) each claiming to bake (D) the city's finest baguette.
options: have been competing with themselves for decades
items.correction: have been competing with each other for decades
items.explanation: Two parties acting on one another need the reciprocal pronoun each other / one another; the reflexive themselves would mean each bakery competes against itself.

items.q: The coach (A) told the reporters that the team (B) had trained all week and that they (C) will be fully prepared (D) for Saturday's final.
items.explanation: In reported speech after a past reporting verb (told) the tenses shift back, so will becomes would.

items.q: The sculptor (A) is renowned (B) for her remarkable ability (C) to turn discarded scrap metal (D) to lifelike animals.
items.explanation: Transformation is expressed with turn something into something else; turn to means to seek help or to face a direction.

items.q: (A) What impresses me most about the design are (B) its simplicity: (C) a single sheet of steel (D) folded into a chair.
options: What impresses me most about the design are
items.correction: What impresses me most about the design is
items.explanation: A what-clause subject is treated as singular, and its complement its simplicity is singular too, so the verb must be is.

items.q: If only the organisers (A) had listened to the residents, (B) the festival would not cause (C) such chaos (D) on the narrow streets last weekend.
options: on the narrow streets last weekend
items.correction: the festival would not have caused
items.explanation: The result happened in the past (last weekend), so after the past-perfect condition the main clause needs would not have caused, the third-conditional form.

items.q: (A) In spite of (B) her limited budget, the young chef (C) succeeded to open (D) a second restaurant within three years.
options: a second restaurant within three years
items.explanation: Succeed is followed by in + -ing, never by a to-infinitive: succeeded in opening.

items.q: (A) Little did the explorers realise (B) that the map they trusted (C) had been drawn by someone (D) who had never set foot to the island.
options: who had never set foot to the island
items.correction: who had never set foot on the island
items.explanation: The idiom is set foot on / in a place; set foot to is not English.
